title: Organizing code with namespaces and using statements
hook: Namespaces give every type a full hierarchical name. Using statements shorten those names in your source — they do not download or load code. Think of them as address shortcuts, not package imports.

blocks.text: A namespace is a logical container for type names. A class's full identity is Namespace.TypeName (plus which assembly it lives in). Folders on disk are just a convention — the compiler does not infer a namespace from the directory path. A using directive tells the compiler "when I write SqsEnvelope, I mean Acme.Messaging.SqsEnvelope." It is compile-time name resolution only.

entries.plainDefinition: A dotted hierarchy (like Acme.Workers) that groups related types and prevents name collisions.
entries.example: System.Collections.Generic.List<T> lives in the System.Collections.Generic namespace.

entries.plainDefinition: A line at the top of a file that imports a namespace so you can use short type names.
entries.example: using System.Text.Json; lets you write JsonSerializer instead of the full name.

entries.plainDefinition: A using that applies to every file in the project, often generated by ImplicitUsings.
entries.example: global using System; is injected automatically in new console apps.

blocks.text: Namespaces keep large codebases readable and prevent two libraries from defining OrderProcessor in the same global scope. File-scoped namespaces (namespace Acme.Workers;) reduce brace noise in modern C#. Global usings cut repetition across files. But overusing global usings can hide where a type actually lives — a problem in shared libraries where you want dependencies visible. Remember: using never adds a NuGet package. You still need a project reference or package reference for the assembly that contains the type.

blocks.title: Folder vs namespace
blocks.body: Moving a .cs file to a different folder does not change its namespace. Only the namespace declaration (or file-scoped namespace line) changes the type's full name.

items.title: Declare a namespace
items.body: namespace Acme.Messaging; applies to all types in the file (file-scoped form).

items.title: Add using directives
items.body: using System.Text.Json; imports the namespace for name lookup in this file.

items.title: Write short names
items.body: JsonSerializer.Serialize(...) resolves because System.Text.Json is in scope.

items.title: CLR sees the full name
items.body: At run time the type is still Acme.Messaging.SqsEnvelope regardless of which usings you wrote.

diagram.title: Namespace vs using
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  A[Type declared in namespace Acme.Workers] --> B[Full name: Acme.Workers.SqsEnvelope]
  C[using Acme.Workers in another file] --> D[Short name: SqsEnvelope]
  E[Project/NuGet reference] --> F[Assembly containing the type]
  F --> B
  D -.->|compile-time only| B

snippet.label: File-scoped namespace
snippet.explanation: File-scoped namespace avoids wrapping the entire file in braces. The type's identity is set by the namespace line, not the directory path.

snippet.label: Using alias and static import
snippet.explanation: using can create aliases (Json = ...) or import static members (using static). Both are compile-time shortcuts.

snippet.label: Global using in a shared project
snippet.explanation: Global usings apply project-wide. Implicit usings generate a similar file automatically. Use explicit global usings when you want control.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming the folder path is the namespace (Java package muscle memory). Adding a using without a package reference and wondering why restore did nothing. Two global using aliases that collide after a SDK bump of implicit usings.

interviewTakeaways: `using` is compile-time name resolution; the assembly reference is a separate project concern.
File-scoped namespaces are equivalent to a block namespace wrapping the file.
`global using` is compilation-wide; overuse hides where a type actually lives.
commonPitfalls: Assuming the folder path is the namespace (Java package muscle memory).
Adding `using` without a package reference and wondering why restore did nothing.
Two `global using` aliases that collide after a SDK bump of implicit usings.

jsTsCorrelations.note: import both names and loads a module. C# using only shortens names; loading is handled by assembly references.
TypeScript namespace is mostly legacy; ES modules are the unit. C# namespaces remain the primary grouping for types inside assemblies.
